newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Human walls block Taiwan premier from parliament.
newsitem.headline: Human walls block Taiwan premier from parliament.

text.p: Opposition deputies on Tuesday formed human walls to prevent Premier Lien Chan from entering parliament where he planned to appeal for restoration of funding for Taiwan's ill-starred fourth nuclear power project.
"This is a dark day for democracy," Lien was quoted by the state-funded Central News Agency as saying after the rebuff.
An angry Lien gave a "thumbs down" gesture before being whisked away by limousine.
"I feel deep regret for what happened today," Lien said. "This is unreasonable. The cabinet should have its dignity. They should try to convince people with reasons, not force."
Lien had planned to deliver a report explaining Taiwan's energy policy and the island's need for a fourth nuclear station as parliament resumed debate on the project.

But dozens of opposition lawmakers, cheered by thousands of anti-nuclear demonstrators, donned green headbands and locked arms to form human walls outside the building's doors, preventing Lien and other officials from entering.
Lien immediately returned to his office.
Lawmakers voted later to adjourn Tuesday's session. A final decision was expected on Friday.
Hanging in the balance is a US$1.8 billion contract awarded to U.S. giant General Electric to supply the power plant's twin reactors and turbines.

Parliament on May 24 dealt an embarrassing blow to the government, halting the 2,700-megawatt plant's US$4.1 billion budget on the very day of state-run Taiwan Power Co's final tender for the facility's two reactors, which GE won.
The cabinet formally appealed the cancellation on June 6 but can be thwarted by a two-thirds vote of parliament -- something Lien and other officials are determined to avoid.

Analysts were reluctant to say whether opponents could muster the votes necessary to make the cancellation stand, a move that experts said would be equivalent to a no-confidence vote with grave implications for Lien.
The row has political implications beyond nuclear power.
It reflects a constitutional showdown between the executive and legislative branches over the constitutionality of Lien serving simultaneously as vice president and premier, or cabinet chief.
Lien was elected vice president in March as running mate of President Lee Teng-hui in a historic election that gave both their first popular mandate. They won in a landslide.

But opposition to his holding both seats runs strong in the Legislative Yuan, or parliament, where the ruling Nationalist party holds a knife-edge 51 percent majority. A constitutional tribunal is reviewing the opponents' challenge.
Taipower, which has continued with work despite the deadlock and regards the nuclear project alive unless a final rejection is approved, asked GE in September to start work.
The utility, calling the plant necessary and safe, already has poured more than US$220 million into its construction.

Taiwan approved the plant in 1994 after years of delays and protests sparked by the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in the then Soviet Union. A growing number of opponents in increasingly democratic Taiwan say nuclear power is dangerous and unnecessary if alternative energy sources are pursued.
